title: Thucydides, Histories, ed. H. Stuart Jones (Perseus tlg0003.tlg001.perseus-grc2)
rights: Ancient text public domain; Perseus digital edition CC BY-SA 4.0
finding: 1.25.4: the Corcyraeans were at times elated 'in accordance with the earlier settlement of Corcyra by the Phaeacians, who had fame in matters of ships' (κατὰ τὴν Φαιάκων προενοίκησιν τῆς Κερκύρας κλέος ἐχόντων τὰ περὶ τὰς ναῦς), and had 120 triremes; Thucydides reports the claim and does not assert it himself. 3.70.4: Peithias accuses the five richest men of cutting vine-props 'from the precinct of Zeus and that of Alcinous' (ἐκ τοῦ τε Διὸς τοῦ τεμένους καὶ τοῦ Ἀλκίνου), a stater per prop; 3.70.5-6: they sit as suppliants and then kill Peithias in the council. 6.2.1: the Cyclopes and Laestrygonians are said to be the oldest inhabitants of part of Sicily; Thucydides cannot say their race or where they came from and refers to the poets. title: Homeric Hymn 3, To Apollo, ed. H. G. Evelyn-White (Perseus tlg0013.tlg003.perseus-grc2)
rights: Ancient text public domain; Perseus digital edition CC BY-SA 4.0
finding: 14-18: Artemis is born on Ortygia, Apollo on rocky Delos beside the palm and the streams of the Inopus. 113-119: when Eileithyia comes to Delos, labour seizes Leto; 'she threw her arms around the palm and pressed her knees into the soft meadow' (ἀμφὶ δὲ φοίνικι βάλε πήχεε, γοῦνα δʼ ἔρεισε λειμῶνι μαλακῷ, 117-118), and Apollo is born. 146-150: the Ionians gather on Delos for boxing, dance and song. This is the earliest consulted text that links a Delian palm with Leto.

title: Strabo, Geography, ed. A. Meineke (Perseus tlg0099.tlg001.perseus-grc2)
rights: Ancient text public domain; Perseus digital edition CC BY-SA 4.0
finding: 1.2.18: Strabo quotes νήσῳ ἐν Ὠγυγίῃ, ὅθι τʼ ὀμφαλός ἐστι θαλάσσης, the daughter of Atlas, and the Phaeacians' οἰκέομεν δʼ ἀπάνευθε πολυκλύστῳ ἐνὶ πόντῳ ἔσχατοι (Od. 6.204-205) as clearly invented in the Atlantic sea. 1.2.37 and 7.3.6: Apollodorus, following Eratosthenes, blames Callimachus, a scholar, for calling Gaudos Calypso's island and Corcyra Scheria. 6.2.4: Archias left Chersicrates to settle 'the island now called Corcyra, formerly Scheria' (τὴν νῦν Κέρκυραν καλουμένην, πρότερον δὲ Σχερίαν). 6.2.11: Melite and Gaudos lie off Pachynus, 88 miles from the cape. 9.2.18: Boeotia was once called Ogygia.

title: Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica, ed. G. W. Mooney (Perseus tlg0001.tlg001.perseus-grc2)
rights: Ancient text public domain; Perseus digital edition CC BY-SA 4.0
finding: 4.537-551: Heracles came to the house of Nausithous and to Macris to wash away the murder of his children; Hyllus, son of the Naiad Melite, would not live under Nausithous' rule, gathered Phaeacians and went to the Cronian sea, Nausithous preparing his journey; the Mentores killed him. 4.948-955: the Nereids toss the Argo between them like girls playing with a ball on a sandy beach. 4.982-992: an island in the Ionian strait under which lies the sickle (of Cronus, or of Demeter), hence Drepane, 'holy nurse of the Phaeacians' (Φαιήκων ἱερὴ τροφός); the Phaeacians are of the blood of Uranus. 4.1011-1029: Medea supplicates Arete (γουνοῦμαι, βασίλεια). 4.1068-1109: Alcinous and Arete discuss Medea at night; he will give her back to her father if she is a virgin but not part her from a husband. 4.1110-1160: Arete's herald to Jason; the wedding in Macris' cave on the Fleece, 'still called the sacred cave of Medea' (1128-1160). 4.1217-1223: Arete gives Medea twelve Phaeacian slave women (δμωὰς Φαιηκίδας ἐκ μεγάροιο, 1221-1222); they leave Drepane. Apollonius does not name Corcyra.

title: Scholia Graeca in Homeri Odysseam, ed. G. Dindorf, vol. 1 (Oxford 1855)
locator: p. 294, schol. on Od. 6.3-9 (page image read)
finding: Schol. 6.4 reports that Hypereia was identified with Camarina in Sicily, explained as 'beyond the known land', or taken as a former island near the Cyclopes; a Thessalian spring has the same name. Schol. 6.8 gives Aristarchus' reading εἷσε δὲ Σχερίῃ and his note that the land was called Scheria, not Corcyra, and lay outside the inhabited world; schol. 6.3 (E) calls it Corcyra; ἀλφηστάων is glossed 'inventive and provident men'. Schol. E on 6.3 calls the land Corcyra; the Aristarchean note on 6.8 says it was named Scheria, not Corcyra, and lay outside the inhabited world; schol. 6.4 on Hypereia (Camarina, 'beyond', an island near the Cyclopes). 6.3: δῆμος is the body of men, πόλις the buildings. 6.4: Hypereia = Camarina in Sicily, or named from ὑπέρ 'beyond the known land', or an island near the Cyclopes; also a spring in Thessaly. 6.7: ἀναστήσας = ἀποικίαν στειλάμενος. 6.8: the Aristarchean copies read εἷσεν δὲ Σχερίῃ, not ἐν Σχερίῃ; Scheria is the name of the Phaeacians' land and not Corcyra, and it is outside the inhabited world. 6.3: the land is the island now called Corcyra (E). 6.7: ἀναστήσας = having sent out a colony (H). 6.8: Aristarchus reads εἷσεν δὲ Σχερίῃ; Scheria, not Corcyra, outside the inhabited world (E.P.Q.).

title: Scholia Graeca in Homeri Odysseam, ed. G. Dindorf, vol. 1 (Oxford 1855)
locator: p. 297, schol. on Od. 6.40, 6.42, 6.44, 6.45, 6.46 (page image read)
finding: Schol. 6.42: ὅθι φασί fits the mountain, not the sky, and marks inherited tradition. Schol. 6.44: Olympus is snowless above and snowy below the clouds; Rhianus read αἰθήρ for αἴθρη. Schol. 6.46: Rhianus read τῇ ἔνι. 6.42 (E.Q.): ὅθι φασί well put of the mountain, badly of heaven; the poet shows a received tradition. 6.44 (B.H.P.Q.T.): snowless above, ἀγάννιφος below the clouds; Rhianus αἰθήρ (H.P.). 6.45 (E.P.Q.V.): ἀνέφελος; heaven from the clouds to the stars. 6.46: Rhianus τῇ ἔνι (H.P.). ὅθι φασί: badly put if of heaven, well put if of the mountain; shows tradition. Olympus snowless above, ἀγάννιφος below the clouds. πλυνοί: the stones on which they wash, or by synecdoche the whole place (B); the places where they wash clothes (E); gloss γοῦρναι (H).

title: Scholia Graeca in Homeri Odysseam, ed. G. Dindorf, vol. 1 (Oxford 1855)

title: Scholia Graeca in Homeri Odysseam, ed. G. Dindorf, vol. 1 (Oxford 1855)
locator: pp. 307-308, schol. on Od. 6.157, 6.159, 6.160, 6.163 (Dindorf's lemma number for the palm note), 6.164, 6.167 (page images read)
finding: Schol. E.V. identify the palm with the one that grew for Leto's labour; schol. B.P.Q. deny it. Schol. 6.164 (E) puts Odysseus' visit to Delos with Menelaus to fetch the daughters of Anius (Oinotropoi) and cites Simonides' Kateuchai. E.V.: the palm that sprang up for Leto; B.P.Q.: not Leto's palm, νέον with ἀνερχόμενον. 6.164 (E): the expedition; Menelaus and Odysseus came to Delos for the daughters of Anius (Simonides). E.P.Q.V.: Odysseus presents himself as a man of rank, not a merchant or rower. E: ἀειθαλὲς φυτόν; he means the palm that sprang up for Leto, which she grasped in giving birth. B.P.Q.: νέον with ἀνερχόμενον, cf. Il. 18.56; οὐ τὸν ἐπὶ τῇ Λητοῖ ἀναδοθέντα φοίνικά φησιν. B.P.: a tree straight by nature. 159: he leads her home having outweighed the other suitors with bride-gifts; the poet flatteringly shows her as much fought over (P.Q.); ἔδνα = gifts before marriage, wooing gifts (V); βρίσας = πολλὰ βαρύνας (B). 157: χορὸν εἰσοιχνεῦσαν = entering the dance, i.e. the gathering of the people (B).

title: Scholia Graeca in Homeri Odysseam, ed. G. Dindorf, vol. 1 (Oxford 1855)
locator: p. 311, schol. on Od. 6.201 and 6.204 (page image read)
finding: Schol. 6.201: Aristarchus takes διερός as 'living'; Callistratus wrote δυερός 'wretched' (from δύη); a gloss gives 'harmful, piratical'. Schol. 6.204 (E.P.Q.T.) says the Phaeacians live in Corcyra and are 'last' relative to Greece; schol. P.T. say the poet places them far away, not at Corcyra. P.T.: the poet places the Phaeacians' land far away, not at Corcyra. E.P.Q.T.: 'and yet they live in Corcyra'; ἔσχατοι is relative to Greece.

title: Scholia Graeca in Homeri Odysseam, ed. G. Dindorf, vol. 1 (Oxford 1855)
finding: ἐπίστιον is glossed ἐποίκιον, σκηνή, νεώριον or σκάφος and derived 'from ἱστίον' (sail); schol. Q calls the psilosis Ionic and also gives a 'hearth' sense. Schol. 6.264 (p. 315, OCR only) reports that Aristophanes wrote ἴσθμη. 6.262: the sentence continues at 289 (H.Q.T.) or at 291 (H.Q.). 6.264: the narrow passage of the harbor, narrowed by the many ships; each Phaeacian owns a ship in which he lodges; Aristophanes wrote ἴσθμη. 6.266: the agora is around the shrine of Poseidon (B.Q.); Ποσιδήϊον = a precinct dedicated to Poseidon (E.V.). 6.267: ῥυτοῖσι = too large to carry, hauled; κατωρυχέεσσι = well founded (B.Q.T.).

title: Eustathius, Commentarii ad Homeri Odysseam, ed. G. Stallbaum, vol. 1 (Leipzig 1825)
locator: vol. 1 pp. 241-242 (Rome p. 1553-1554), on Od. 6.100-119 (p. 241 page image and OCR; p. 242 OCR)
finding: p. 241: the girls threw off their veils and played simply, with bare heads; the ball fell into the deep, not by the banks, so the women cried out and Odysseus woke from the long cry, not from the song; the ancients praised the passage for brevity. Later, 'they say', ball play was cultivated most by the Lacedaemonians among cities, by Alexander the Great among kings, and by Sophocles among private men, 'who, they say, when he produced the Plyntriai, won great acclaim acting the part of Nausicaa playing ball' (ὅτε φασὶ τὰς Πλυντρίας ἐδίδασκε, τὸ τῆς Ναυσικάας πρόσωπον σφαίρᾳ παιζούσης ὑποκρινόμενος, ἰσχυρῶς εὐδοκίμησεν); σφαῖρα derived from σπάω or from αἴρω; σφαιρομαχεῖν and σφαιρίζειν in Plato. p. 242: Dionysodorus wrote πάλλαν for σφαῖραν (6.115); Latin pila; whether the game is the one called ἐφετίνδα, in which the ball is shown to one player and thrown to another; also called φεννίς (OCR).

title: Eustathius, Commentarii ad Homeri Odysseam, ed. G. Stallbaum, vol. 1 (Leipzig 1825)
locator: vol. 1 pp. 251-252, on Od. 6.240-248 (paraphrase on p. 251; glosses of δέατο and ἅδοι on p. 252)

title: Eustathius, Commentarii ad Homeri Odysseam, ed. G. Stallbaum, vol. 1 (Leipzig 1825)
finding: ἐπίστιον is Ionic and unaspirated, derived from ἱστία (= ἑστία), and also called νεώριον, a ship-house; Eustathius compares Herodotus' ἐπίστιος for ἐφέστιος. ἐπίστιον 'something like ἐποίκιον'; Ionic, so unaspirated; cf. Hdt. ἐπίστιος for ἐφέστιος; from ἱστία (= ἑστία); also called νεώριον and νεῶν οἶκοι; Aelius Dionysius: Ionic νεῶνες, Attic νεώσοικοι.

title: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. 1, Books I-XII, 2nd ed. (Oxford 1886)
finding: M&R call Hypereia and Scheria topographical descriptions ('Highlands', 'Coast') and trace the Corcyra identification to Callimachus (via Strabo 7.3.6) and Thucydides 1.25, 3.70; they report the scholion story that Scheria was first called Drepane. A passage of Odysseus' tales seems to place Scheria off the Thesprotian coast, which may have given rise to the Corcyra identification (Callimachus in Strabo 7.3.6; Thuc. 1.25; 3.70). 'When we attempt to establish the identity, the story melts into romance.' Hypereia and Scheria = 'Highlands' and 'Coast'. Schol. E: Scheria first called Drepane (the sickle of Cronus), later Scheria from σχεῖν, because Poseidon stopped a flood at Demeter's request. 'The wonderland of the West'. Hypereia and Scheria descriptive names; the Thesprotian hints may have given rise to the Corcyra tradition; 'the story melts into romance'.

title: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. 1, Books I-XII, 2nd ed. (Oxford 1886)
locator: pp. 39-40, note on Od. 1.347-349 (the discussion of ἀλφηστῇσιν is on p. 40)
finding: Two derivations of ἀλφηστής: from the root ἀλφ- 'earn' (ἀλφάνω, ἀλφεσίβοιαι), 'gain-getting', contrasted with θεοὶ ῥεῖα ζώοντες, cf. Aesch. Seven 770 (favoured); or from ἄλφι + ἔδω 'bread-eating', cf. σιτοφάγος Od. 9.191, Il. 6.142, and the sense intended in Soph. Phil. 707-709. The grammarians' glosses συνετοί, εὑρετικοί, ἐπινοητικοί suit the first.

title: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. 1, Books I-XII, 2nd ed. (Oxford 1886)
locator: pp. 255-257, notes on Od. 6.40-47 (Lucretius, Tennyson and the other parallels on p. 256)
finding: M&R compare Lucretius 3.18 ff., Lucan 2.271 and Seneca De Ira 3.6 with the Olympus passage, and report that Aristarchus took Homer's Olympus as the mountain. Quotes Lucr. 3.18 ff.; Lucan 2.271; Seneca De Ira 3.6; 'Tennyson imitates the passage in his Morte d'Arthur, describing the island valley of Avilion'; Coleridge's Hymn in the Vale of Chamouni; Eustathius on snowless upper Olympus. ὅθι φασί cf. Il. 2.783, 24.615; schol. E.Q. vs Eustathius; Köchly takes the passage as a later insertion; M&R think this too strong. Epithets of Olympus in Homer. Aristarchus: Homer always means the mountain. Clouds as boundary, summit clear (Eustathius). Lucan 2.271, Lucretius 3.18 ff., Seneca De Ira 3.6, Tennyson Morte d'Arthur, Coleridge. ἕδος ἀσφαλὲς αἰεί cf. Pindar Nem. 6. ἀνέφελος better than ἀννέφελος. Critical notes: Rhianus αἰθήρ (44), τῇ ἔνι (46).

title: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. 1, Books I-XII, 2nd ed. (Oxford 1886)
finding: The Delos visit is placed on the voyage from Aulis to Troy; M&R cite the scholion on Leto's palm, Euripides Hecuba 458, Cicero De Legibus 1.1.2 and Pliny NH 16. The visit to Delos seems to belong to the voyage from Aulis to Troy through the Cyclades; a palm was kept in the precinct; the scholion refers to Leto's palm; Cicero De Legibus 1.1.2 and Pliny report the palm still shown. The visit belongs to the voyage from Aulis to Troy through the Cyclades; a palm preserved in the Delian precinct; schol. on Leto's palm, Eur. Hec. 458; Cicero Leg. 1.1.2; Pliny NH 16.99.44 (= 16.240). Visit on the voyage from Aulis; a palm always preserved in the precinct, like the μορίαι in the Academy (Soph. OC 705); schol. on Leto's palm, Eur. Hec. 458; Cicero says the palm was still to be seen.

title: V. A. Chernysheva, 'Sappho 1.1-4 L.-P.: Throne or Patterns?', Philologia Classica 12.2 (2017) 231-233, doi 10.21638/11701/spbu20.2017.211
finding: εὔθρονος is used of Eos alone (Il. 8.565; Od. 6.48; 15.495; 17.497); Wustmann (1868) derived -θρονος from θρόνα 'patterns', a view applied by the author to Sappho's ποικιλόθρονος, not to Homeric ἐύθρονος. εὔθρονος at Il. 8.565, Od. 6.48, 15.495, 17.497, of Eos only; Wustmann (RhM 23, 1868, 238) derived -θρονος from θρόνα 'patterns'; supported by Aly 1920 and Burnett 1983, rejected by Wilamowitz 1913; her argument concerns Sappho's ποικιλόθρονος, not Homeric ἐύθρονος.

title: P. Merciai, review of S. E. Psoma, Corcyra: a city at the edge of two Greek worlds (2022), BMCR 2024.05.19
finding: Psoma discusses the identification of Corcyra with Homeric Scheria in chapter 14; the review cites remains of early 7th-century BC shipsheds and questions Psoma's reading of a coin type as an allusion to Od. 10.410-415. Psoma discusses the identification with Scheria (bibliography in notes, chapter 14 on the legendary traditions). Shipsheds of the early 7th century BC attest Corcyra's early sea power (chapter 3).

title: A. Kelly, review of J. Arft, Arete and the Odyssey's Poetics of Interrogation (2022), BMCR 2024.03.15
locator: whole review (paragraphs on chapters 3-4 and the conclusion)
finding: Arft treats Nausicaa's marriageability as central and reads her as resolute and active (pp. 118-130); the reviewer notes that Odysseus' recapitulation to Penelope (Od. 23.338-341) does not mention Nausicaa. Arft reads Arete's question 'who gave you these clothes?' (7.237-238) as central to the Phaeacian episode and treats Nausicaa's marriageability as central; the reviewer notes that 23.338-341 does not mention Nausicaa.

title: J. Holoka, review of C. Segal, Singers, Heroes, and Gods in the Odyssey (1994), BMCR 1995.06.14
finding: Segal reads the Phaeacian episode as a transition between the fabulous world and Ithaca, contrasting Ogygia's isolation with Scheria's community; the essays include 'The Phaeacians and Odysseus' Return'. Segal reads the Phaeacian episode as transitional: Odysseus is 'on his way back to mortality but not yet fully involved in it' (Segal p. 18, as quoted by the reviewer). Segal's book was not opened directly.

title: Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon (9th ed. 1940), Perseus XML

Op. 82); esp. traders or seafarers (13.261; h.Ap. 458); of the Phaeacians, 6.8. Twice in tragedy (A. Th. 770; S. Ph. 709). ἀλφάνω 'bring in, yield' (Od. 17.250).

title: Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon (9th ed. 1940), Perseus XML

Aristarch. ad loc.; but perh. for δϝι-ερός 'to be feared'); διερῷ ποδί 'with nimble foot' 9.43. After Hom. wet, liquid (A. Eu. 263; Anaxag. 4, 12). Sense I perh. cogn. with δίεμαι; sense II prob. with διαίνω.

title: Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon (9th ed. 1940), Perseus XML

Il. 2.125) as Ionic for ἐφέστιον, but Homer elsewhere always ἐφέστιος; scholia ἐποίκιον, νεώριον, from ἱστίον. ἐφέστιος 'at one's own fireside' (Od. 3.234, 7.248, 23.55; Il. 2.125); Ionic ἐπίστιος in Hdt.

title: Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae, ed. G. Kaibel (Perseus tlg0008.tlg001.perseus-grc3)
rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 (licence element in the file); ancient text public domain
finding: 1.14d: Homer has dances of tumblers and dances with the ball; Agallis of Corcyra, a woman grammarian (γραμματική), gives the invention of the ball to Nausicaa 'as a favour to her fellow citizen' (ὡς πολίτιδι χαριζομένη), Dicaearchus to the Sicyonians, Hippasus to the Lacedaemonians together with the gymnasia; ταύτην δὲ μόνην τῶν ἡρωίδων Ὅμηρος παράγει σφαιρίζουσαν. 1.14d-15a then names Demoteles and Chaerephanes, the follicle of Atticus of Naples for Pompey, harpaston = phaininda, and Antiphanes' ball-game calls. This passage does not mention Sophocles. Casaubon letters confirmed by LSJ citations of Ath. 1.14d and 1.14f.

title: Plutarch, Quomodo adulescens poetas audire debeat, ed. G. N. Bernardakis (Perseus tlg0007.tlg068.perseus-grc2)
rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 (licence element in the file); ancient text public domain
finding: 'Where the poet's judgement is unclear, one must make a distinction' (ὅπου δʼ ἀσαφῆ τὰ τῆς γνώμης, διοριστέον): if Nausicaa, feeling τὸ τῆς Καλυψοῦς πάθος for a stranger, ἅτε δὴ τρυφῶσα καὶ γάμων ὥραν ἔχουσα, talks such folly, her boldness and licence must be blamed; if she saw his character in his words and prays for such a husband rather than πλωτικῷ τινι καὶ ὀρχηστικῷ τῶν πολιτῶν, she deserves admiration (27A-B). Plutarch quotes 6.244-245 with ἐμεῦ for ἐμοί. The same section quotes Il. 9.458-461 (Phoenix, with δήμου φάτιν καὶ ὀνείδεα) and says Aristarchus removed the lines; it goes on to Penelope's gifts (Od. 18.282), the counting of the treasure (Od. 13.216) and the sleep on landing.

title: Cicero, De Legibus, book 1, The Latin Library
locator: 1.1-2 (The Latin Library section [2]; the palm sentence in 1.2)
finding: Quintus says that the Marian oak will last as long as Latin letters, 'nisi forte Athenae tuae sempiternam in arce oleam tenere potuerunt, aut quam Homericus Ulixes Deli se proceram et teneram palmam vidisse dixit, hodie monstrant eandem'; many things last longer in memory than they could stand in nature. The remark is ironic: poetry outlasts nature.

title: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura (Perseus phi0550.phi001.perseus-lat1)
rights: Ancient text public domain; Perseus digital edition CC BY-SA 4.0
finding: Praise of Epicurus (3.1-17); 3.18-22: apparet divum numen sedesque quietae, which no winds shake, no clouds sprinkle with rain, no snow defiles, while a cloudless upper air (innubilus aether) covers them and laughs with light spread wide (large diffuso lumine ridet); 3.23-24: nature supplies everything and nothing takes away their peace of mind; 3.25: nowhere do the regions of Acheron appear. title: Scholia Graeca in Homeri Odysseam, ed. G. Dindorf, vol. 1 (Oxford 1855)
finding: 6.12 (B.P.Q.): the poet hints that Odysseus will meet a hospitable man. 6.18 (P.): the beauty of the two handmaids prepares 'all are beautiful' (6.108), which does not suit slave bodies; (D.) the two handmaids slept beside her. 6.22: accent of ναυσικλειτοῖο; some read Ναυσικλειτοῖ, a name in the dative like Καλυψοῖ, others ναυσὶ κλειτοῖο in two words; the first is better, 'famous in naval works' (P.Q.). 6.23 ὁμηλικίη = ὁμῆλιξ (H.). 6.53 (Q.T.): though the polity is most luxurious she does not neglect work; sea-purple suits a queen, as Helen works violet wool. 6.57 πάππα: a lisping, affectionate address of a younger to an older person (E.P.); a list of such addresses, τέττα to a friend, ἄττα to a foster father, θεῖε to an uncle, πάππα to a father (E.). 6.60 (P.Q.T.): Athena spoke of marriage openly; Nausicaa transfers the need to the father and brothers, but the speech hints at the truth because of her age. 6.65 (H.P.T.): the Phaeacians, living in luxury, danced daily. 6.70 ὑπερτερίῃ: a box or squared timber set on the wagon for the load (B.E.Q.V.). 6.71 δμώεσσιν glossed θεραπαινίσιν (V.); 6.74-75 Aristophanes read φέρον and κατέθηκαν, i.e. the δμῶες carried the clothes (H.P.).txt; pages fixed from the running heads.

title: Scholia Graeca in Homeri Odysseam, ed. G. Dindorf, vol. 1 (Oxford 1855)
finding: 6.162-163 (E.V.): he means the palm that sprang up for Leto, which she held when she gave birth; (B.P.Q.) he does not mean the palm of Leto, reading νέον with ἀνερχόμενον. 6.164 (E.P.Q.V.): Odysseus presents himself as a man of rank, not a merchant or a rower; (E.) the 'great host' is the Greek expedition, when Menelaus with Odysseus came to Delos for the daughters of Anius, called Oinotropoi; the story is also in Simonides' Kateuchai. 6.165 (P.): note on μέλλεν. 6.195 (E.T.): how can the Phaeacians live in Corcyra if they are 'farthest away'? 'Farthest' from Greece. 6.197 (D.E.P.): the affairs of the Phaeacians hang from Alcinous; (P.) 'the Phaeacians' by periphrasis.

title: Scholia Graeca in Homeri Odysseam, ed. G. Dindorf, vol. 1 (Oxford 1855)
finding: 6.293 (E.V.): τέμενος, land cut off as an honor. 6.302 (B.): with a vocative ἥρως the words are addressed to Odysseus. 6.305 (E.): ἐπ' ἐσχάρῃ means a higher seat, not 'beside the hearth'; (B., H.) it shows the season, that it was winter. 6.310 (E.H.Q.V., citing Callistratus): he is to supplicate the mother either because a woman favors a woman, or because Arete is handed down as most sensible, and the female is otherwise more compassionate; (T.) she bids him appeal to the woman as compassionate. 6.330 (B.): πατροκασίγνητον is Poseidon, brother of her father Zeus; Aristarchus accented ζαφελῶς with a circumflex. 6.291: variant δήομεν, γρ. δήεις (the more elegant copies δήεις); ἄγχι θαλάσσης with γρ. κελεύθου (H). 6.293: τέμενος = land cut off as an honor; ἀλωή = land for planting. 6.305: ἐπ' ἐσχάρῃ means seated higher, by the fire; it was winter (B, H). 6.310: Odysseus is sent to the queen because a woman favors a woman, or because Arete is the wisest; the female is compassionate (Callistratus). 6.321: δύσετο = was declining to the west (P.Q.T.). 6.329: γρ. ἄζετο (P). 6.330: πατροκασίγνητον = Poseidon, brother of her father Zeus (B); Aristarchus accented ζαφελῶς as a perispomenon.

title: Scholia Graeca in Homeri Odysseam, ed. G. Dindorf, vol. 1 (Oxford 1855)
finding: 7.53 (B.P.Q.T.): how does Athena's 'you will find the mistress first' agree with Nausicaa's 'pass him by'? κιχήσεαι means 'you will supplicate'. 7.54 (P.V.): Arete, because she was born in answer to prayer; ἐπώνυμον glossed φερώνυμον (V.). 7.54-55 (E.P.Q.): 'from the same parents' conflicts with Rhexenor as her father; τοκῆες can mean ancestors; (B.) so they are uncle and niece; (B.P.Q.T.) Hesiod took Arete to be the sister of Alcinous. (P.Q.) The genealogy lets the suppliant address her by her father's name (7.146).

title: Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon (9th ed. 1940), Perseus XML
locator: s.vv. ἀρατός, ἀρητός, δμῳή, δμώς, ὑπερηνορέων, ῥαίω, ἐπιζάφελος, ἠίθεος, ὀπυίω
finding: ἀρατός, Ion. ἀρητός: 'prayed against, accursed' (Il. 17.37) and 'prayed for'; hence the proper names Ἄρητος, Ἀρήτη, 'the Prayed-for'. δμῳή 'or δμωή (both spellings freq. in codd.)', female slave taken in war, generally serving-woman, only plural in Homer (Il. 9.658 cited). δμώς, slave taken in war; dat. pl. δμώεσσι Od. 6.71. ὑπερηνορέων 'overbearing', of the Trojans, of the Cyclopes Od. 6.5, mostly of the suitors. ῥαίω 'shatter'; passive ῥαιόμενος 'suffering shipwreck' Od. 6.326; of a ship 8.569, 13.151. ἐπιζαφελῶς 'vehemently, furiously' Od. 6.330. ἠίθεος 'unmarried youth'. ὀπυίω 'of the man, marry'.

title: Scholia Graeca in Homeri Odysseam, ed. G. Dindorf, vol. 1 (Oxford 1855), Book 6
finding: 6.58 and 6.74: the epithets describe the clothes as clean by nature, not as they then were; 6.60 (P.Q.T.): Athena spoke openly of marriage, Nausicaa turns the need to her father and brothers. 6.70 ὑπερτερίῃ: a πλινθίον set on the wagon for heavier loads (B.P.V.), or the square timber above the wagon that receives the load (B.E.Q.V.); 6.70 εὔκυκλον = εὔτροχον (H); 6.88 variant ἁμάξης for ἀπήνης (H); 6.72 variant ἡμιόνοιν (H). 6.90 ἄγρωστις a grassy herb (V), diuretic (P). 6.318: Callistratus read αἱ δ' εὖ μὲν τρεχέτην; πλίσσοντο = went at a walk, 'they trotted well and walked well' (B.H.P.Q.T.); πλίσσειν = moving leg past leg, Doric πλίκες 'steps', Hippocratic πλίγμα; V: πλίσσοντο = διέβαινον, a hapax. 6.162 (E) evergreen growing plant; (E.V.) the palm that sprang up for Leto; (B.P.Q.) not Leto's palm, νέον with ἀνερχόμενον, cf. Il. 18.56; (B.P.) a tree straight by nature; 6.167 (E) he calls the tree δόρυ; 6.160 (H.P.Q.) we call well-grown people shoots and stems. 6.52 (V) παρὰ τῇ ἐσχάρᾳ, the place where fire is burned; 6.305 ἐπί does not mean 'beside the hearth' but describes the higher seat (cf. Il. 6.15); (B, H) the fire shows it was winter. (Q.T.) though of a most luxurious polity the queen does not neglect work; sea-purple fits a queen, as Helen works violet-dark wool; (B) ἠλάκατα the wool, ἠλακάτη the wood on which it is wound; (H.V.) ἠλάκατα here the wool; (H) ἁλιπόρφυρα sea-dyed. 6.308 ποτικέκλιται αὐγῇ (V): surrounded by the light, i.e. lit up; Dindorf cites Eustathius p. 1564.25 for αὐγῇ ἢ αὐτῇ. Erymanthus a mountain of Arcadia with many boars and deer (B.P.Q.); these places abound in boars and deer; no lions named, since they are not bred there, as Aristotle says (Dindorf refers to H.A. 6.31).

title: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. 1, Books I-XII, 2nd ed. (Oxford 1886)
locator: p. 260, note on 6.86 (πλυνοί); p. 255 note on 6.37; p. 257 note on 6.57; p. 259 notes on 6.70, 6.73, 6.83; p. 259, notes on 6.73, 6.83; p. 260, note on 6.90; pp. 275-278, notes on 6.264, 6.269 (with critical note) and 6.272; p. 259, note on 6.80; p. 266, note on 6.162; p. 257, note on 6.53
finding: The πλυνοί are tanks dug at the side of the river with water flowing in and out. 6.37 ἄμαξα four-wheeled, distinct from the two-wheeled ἅρμα; etymology ἅμα + ἄγω or (Grashof) ἀμφι-ἄξων. 6.57 οὐκ ἂν δή beseeching question; ἀπήνη a four-wheeled load cart drawn by mules or oxen; Lobeck on the synonyms. 6.70 ὑπερτερίη: box for baggage (scholia; cf. πείρινθα Il. 24.267) or hood/awning; ἀραρυῖαν makes 'awning' somewhat more likely. 6.83 ἄμοτον; the maids followed on foot (6.319), so the pace was steady. 6.73 ὕπαγον ὑπ' ἀπήνῃ: necks put under the yoke; 6.83 ἄμοτον from ἀ- + μοτόν (Aristarchus), 'they stepped straight on without flagging'; 6.90 ἄγρωστις clover, couch grass or dog's-tooth grass. 6.264 εἰρύαται: scholia uncertain between 'hauled up' and 'guard the road'; M&R prefer 'are drawn up along the road'. 6.269: variant σπείρας in Eustathius, 'warping-cables' (schol. T); ἀποξύνουσιν cp. προήκεα of oars, Od. 12.205. 6.272 ἀγαλλόμενοι: the personal bond between the Phaeacians and their ships (Od. 8.559). χυτλώσαιτο: χύτλον 'anything poured', technically a mixture of oil and water (ὑδρέλαιον) used by bathers; the verb covers bathing and anointing (6.96). A palm always preserved in the Delian precinct, like the sacred olives of the Academy; cites the scholion, Eur. Hec. 458, Cicero and Pliny. ἠλάκατα 'the yarn' spun off from the distaff, no singular; ἁλιπόρφυρα perhaps an allusion to the Phoenician murex dye.

title: Scholia Graeca in Homeri Odysseam, ed. G. Dindorf, vol. 1 (Oxford 1855)
locator: p. 296, schol. on Od. 6.28, 6.29, 6.31, 6.32 (OCR text with archive.org page index)
finding: 6.28: those who lead her home = the bridegroom (B) or the bridegroom's people, to whom brides gave clothes by custom (Q.T.); the poet prepares the men's clothing so that Odysseus may get some (P.T.); ἄγωνται used properly of leading a wife (B). 6.29: Callistratus read χάρις and said Aristophanes changed it to φάτις (H.P.). 6.32 συνέριθος: properly a woman who works with another at the wool, hence any helper; or a co-worker 'from the good strife' (V).

title: Scholia Graeca in Homeri Odysseam, ed. G. Dindorf, vol. 1 (Oxford 1855)
finding: 6.87: ὑπό shows the water rising from the depth (B.E.). 6.92: βόθροι = the washing pits, the tanks (B.Q.). 6.100: ταὶ δ' ἄρ is the reading of all copies, with δ (H.P.). 6.101: the poet calls the whole game μολπή; the younger critics take it as song; that Nausicaa did not sing but played ball is shown by 6.115 (B.E.H.P.Q.); μολπή = παιδιά, as μέλπηθρα and μέλπεσθαι Ἄρηι (P). 6.86 ἐπηετανοί = many, continuous, lasting the whole year (E). 6.87 the water flows forward to the basins (B.E.H.P.). 6.92 βόθροι = the pools, the tanks (B.Q.). 6.116 (H.P.Q.): the passage is famous for its economy; 'deep' accounts for the shout, the ball having fallen in mid-stream, not by the bank; the long shout makes Odysseus' waking plausible. The passage is among those celebrated for brevity; βαθείῃ explains why the girls cried out (the ball fell into the middle of the stream, not by the bank); μακρὸν ἄυσαν makes the waking of Odysseus plausible.

title: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. 1, Books I-XII, 2nd ed. (Oxford 1886)

title: Eustathius, Commentarii ad Homeri Odysseam, ed. G. Stallbaum, vol. 1 (Leipzig 1825)

title: Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon (9th ed. 1940), Perseus XML
locator: s.vv. πλυνός (n84000), πλύνω (n84008), ἐπηετανός (n38811), συνέριθος (n100400), ἔριθος (n42452)

locator: Preface (dated 27 September 1897); H. Festing Jones' introduction to the 2nd ed.; chapters I, VIII (title), XI 'Who was the writer?', XIII
finding: Butler argues that the Odyssey was written at Trapani by a young woman who put herself into the poem as Nausicaa, and that Scheria and Ithaca are drawn from Trapani (title of chapter VIII). Chapter I: Bentley's remark that the Iliad was written for men and the Odyssey for women. Chapter XI 'Who was the writer?': the writer is Nausicaa (the friend, Dymas' daughter, who would have come washing; 'all Nausicaa, and nothing but Nausicaa'; the ill-natured talk; her absence after Book 8, farewell at 8.460); date c. 1050-1000 BC. Chapter XIII: Thucydides 1.25 'tells us that the inhabitants of Corfu were the descendants of the Phaeacians', and 'the older name of Corfu was Drepane'. Frontispiece 'Nausicaa' = La Musa Polinnia at Cortona. The preface (27 September 1897) says no scholar answered his letters to the Athenaeum (1892) or his Italian pamphlets. Festing Jones' introduction to the second edition quotes Butler's note on the discovery of female authorship at Chiavenna (1891) and of Trapani (1892), names him as author of Erewhon, and gives his death in 1902.
